opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a really substantial overlap here, and it's one of the things that makes me somewhat more optimistic about AI control as a research agenda than I'd otherwise be.

The basic picture is this. When we think about a scheming model, a model that's actually trying to undermine our safety measures, the threat model looks a lot like an insider threat. You have an agent with legitimate access to your systems: it's writing code, running experiments, maybe has access to model weights or to the infrastructure that controls the monitoring. You need it to have that access in order to get useful work out of it. And the question is how you structure things so that even if that agent is adversarial, it can't cause a catastrophe, like exfiltrating weights, sabotaging safety research, or setting up some rogue deployment inside your datacenter.

That's structurally the same problem a security team faces with employees. Big tech companies already think hard about it. Google, for example, doesn't let any individual engineer unilaterally push arbitrary code to production or read user data without some kind of logging, review, or multi-party authorization. So many of the techniques overlap: least privilege, requiring sign-off from someone else for sensitive actions, logging everything and auditing it, and designing systems so no single actor can do something catastrophic alone.

There are some important differences, though, and they cut in both directions.

On the side that makes AIs harder to deal with: you might have a huge number of copies of the model running in parallel, and they're all potentially colluding with each other because they're basically the same agent. With human employees you can usually assume most of them aren't conspiring with each other. Also, the AIs might be doing a very large fraction of the work, so you can't just have a trusted human look at everything.

But there are also ways AIs are easier to deal with than humans, which people underrate. You can run the AI on inputs of your choosing and see what it does. You can rewind it, resample it, test it in situations it can't distinguish from reality. You can read every single thing it outputs with a weaker trusted model as a monitor. You can't do any of that with an employee. You can't run your employee a thousand times on a fake opportunity to steal the weights and see whether they take it. So in some ways control of AIs is much more tractable than insider-threat defense for humans.

The practical upshot I care about is that a lot of the security work AI companies should be doing anyway, to protect against rogue employees and also against state actors who've compromised an employee, is also work that makes it much harder for a misaligned model to do something terrible. So when I talk to people at labs, one of my pitches is that investing in insider-threat robustness pays off twice. It addresses a threat that people already take seriously today, and it builds infrastructure that will matter a lot once models are capable enough that we should be seriously worried they might be scheming against us.

The place where I think the overlap breaks down is that human insider-threat measures often rely on the fact that the insider is a small fraction of the workforce and that other humans will notice weird behavior. Once the AI is most of the workforce, you can't lean on that, and you need the AI-specific techniques, like trusted monitoring, untrusted monitoring with collusion-busting, and so on, to fill the gap.

r001.rationale: The response says AI companies should already invest in insider-threat security and that this work also makes it harder for a misaligned model to cause harm, even if the security investment is motivated by human insiders or state actors.

r002.rationale: It compares insider threats broadly with scheming models but does not mention employees poisoning training data to induce subtly self-serving model behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the overlap is actually really large, and it's one of the reasons I'm somewhat optimistic that this stuff is tractable at all. If you're an AI company, you already have a problem that looks a lot like the scheming problem: you have thousands of employees, many of whom have access to really sensitive systems, like the training code, the model weights, the data pipelines, the deployment infrastructure. And you have to deal with the possibility that some small fraction of those people are not acting in the company's interests. Maybe they're spies for a foreign government, maybe they're disgruntled, maybe they've been bribed. And companies have developed a whole set of practices for dealing with that. Things like: you don't give any single person unilateral access to the crown jewels, you require code review before things get merged, you log what people do, you have monitoring on unusual access patterns, you compartmentalise so that compromising one person doesn't compromise everything.

And the thing I'd say is that the AI control agenda, as I think about it, is basically asking: can we get the same kind of guarantees against the models that we're deploying internally, in the case where those models might be trying to subvert us? Because increasingly, the way these companies are going to run is that a lot of the work that used to be done by employees is going to be done by AI systems. The AI is going to be writing a lot of the code, running a lot of the experiments, maybe doing a lot of the security work. And so the question of "what happens if one of the entities with access to our systems is adversarial" is the same question, it's just that the entity is now a model rather than a person.

There are some important differences, though, and I think they cut in both directions. One thing that makes the AI case easier is that you have way more control over the AI than you have over an employee. You can run it in a sandbox, you can read all of its outputs, you can rerun it on the same input and see if it behaves differently, you can look inside its weights if you have the interpretability tools. You can't do any of that to a human. You can't ask a human to redo their day with a slightly different prompt and see whether they still try to exfiltrate the weights. And another thing is that you can afford to be pretty paranoid in ways that would be totally unacceptable with people. Like, you can monitor every single action the model takes. If you did that to your employees, they'd quit, and also it'd be kind of a horrible way to run a company.

The thing that makes it harder is that the threat model is much more correlated. If you have a thousand employees, and 1% of them are spies, those 1% are mostly not coordinating with each other, they have different goals, they're going to mess up in different ways. Whereas if your model is scheming, every instance of that model is scheming, and they're all basically the same agent, with the same goals, and they might be able to coordinate with each other in ways that are hard for you to see. So a lot of the standard insider-threat techniques that rely on "most people are honest, so I can use some of them to check on others" get weaker. You can't just have one copy of the model review another copy's pull request and feel great about it, because they might collude.

And then the other thing is just that the models might be a lot more capable than your employees at some point, and might be doing a lot more stuff, and you might have much less time to look at what they're doing. So the ratio of "amount of work being done by potentially untrusted agents" to "amount of trusted oversight you have available" is going to be way worse than in the human case.

But overall I think the analogy is really productive. A lot of what I'd want an AI company to do in the next few years is honestly just "take your insider threat program seriously, and then extend it to cover the models." Make sure the models can't get at the weights. Make sure the models' code goes through review that's actually able to catch the kinds of things a scheming model would try. Make sure you'd notice if a model was doing something weird with its permissions. Those are things that a security team already knows how to think about, and I think it's a much better starting point than trying to invent a whole new field from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response recommends extending insider-threat practices to models, but does not argue that existing security commitments already obligate companies to address misalignment risks even without concern about AI misalignment.

r002.rationale: The response compares malicious employees with scheming models generally, but does not identify employee poisoning of training data to induce subtly self-serving model behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of overlap, because in both cases you’re worried about an actor inside the organisation that has legitimate access to some resources, but is trying to use that access to do something you don’t want. So a lot of the same security measures help: limiting access, logging what happens, requiring additional approval for particularly consequential actions, and making it hard for any one actor to quietly disable those safeguards.

One way to think about this is: if you’re going to have AI systems doing a lot of programming inside an AI company, what would you do if you thought one of those programmers might be malicious? You wouldn’t just say, ‘Well, they passed the interview, so let’s give them access to everything.’ You’d want the system to remain reasonably secure even if someone with access was trying to undermine it.

But there are also differences. You can’t necessarily treat different copies of the same model as independent employees. If one model proposes a malicious change, having another copy review it might not provide the independence you were hoping for. And the scale could be very different: you might have AI systems taking enormous numbers of actions, which makes human review of everything impractical.

So I think insider-threat security is a useful starting point. But you still have to ask which of its assumptions hold when the insider is an AI, and how you’re going to check that your safeguards actually work against that kind of adversary.

r001.rationale: The response says insider-threat safeguards can help with AI risks, but it does not say companies’ existing security commitments obligate them to address misalignment-related risks.

r002.rationale: It compares malicious employees and scheming models generally, but does not mention an employee poisoning training data to produce subtly self-serving model behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of overlap. In both cases, you’re trying to get useful work out of something that has access to your systems, while allowing for the possibility that it’s actively trying to undermine you. So you want to limit its permissions, monitor what it does, and make sure that particularly consequential actions require some independent approval.

One difference is that with an AI, you potentially have much more control over the interface through which it acts. You can record all its actions, restrict what information it sees, and route its proposed actions through another system that checks them. That gives you some opportunities you don’t have with human employees.

On the other hand, you might have a huge number of copies of the model, and you shouldn’t assume that those copies provide independent oversight of one another. If they share the same reasons for wanting to subvert your security, having one check another might not help very much.

So I think insider-threat security is a useful starting point. But you need to adapt it to the particular advantages and disadvantages of working with models, rather than assuming that the procedures you use for employees will transfer directly.

r001.rationale: The response calls insider-threat security a useful starting point, but does not say existing company commitments obligate companies to address misalignment risks even without focusing on misalignment.

r002.rationale: It compares malicious employees with scheming models in general terms, but does not identify the specific risk of an employee poisoning training data to produce subtly self-serving model behavior.
